children: US soybean futures slid to a fresh two-month low on Tuesday while corn fell to a 2-1/2 month low on fund long liquidation and pressure from active harvesting of what are expected to be bumper US crops.
Wheat futures followed corn and soybeans lower, sinking to the lowest point since mid-July on fund selling and slumping demand.

Forecasts for continued favourable harvest weather in the Midwest through at least the end of this week dragged down crop markets as farmers gathered a record-large soy harvest and what is projected to be the second-largest corn crop on record.
The harvest pressure overshadowed renewed Chinese demand for US soybeans as the US Department of Agriculture confirmed more purchases by the world's top importer.

"The Chinese have been buying, but the problem is they're buying the 25 million (metric tons) that we knew they were going to buy. It seems like it is now baked into the cake," said Jim McCormick, chief operating officer at AgMarket.
"At this point, you're just getting kind of your traditional hedge pressure being magnified by some fund liquidation."

Chicago Board of Trade November soybeans (SX26) were down 7-1/4 cents at $12.46-1/4 a bushel at 11:57 a.m. CDT (1657 GMT), the lowest since August 26. December corn (CZ26) fell 5-3/4 cents to $4.61-1/4 a bushel, the contract's lowest point since August 12.
Harvesting of both crops was slightly behind the average pace, but forecasters expect dry conditions through at least the rest of this week that will boost field work progress.
The USDA said 44% of the US corn crop was harvested as of Sunday, short of the five-year average of 52% for this point of the season. The soybean harvest was 64% complete, a point below average.
CBOT December wheat (WZ26) was down 12 cents at $6.43-1/4 a bushel, its lowest since July 10.
